summary: Shows the build context carried by signed artifact claims: workflow, repository, organization, environment, commit, triggering event, and OIDC information. It connects those claims to consumer-defined acceptance policy and explains how an SBOM can accompany provenance.
defensive_use: Separate the question of where an artifact came from from whether its source and build process meet release requirements. Compare the expected build identity with recorded provenance before accepting a release. Treat claims from build infrastructure as evidence that still needs an explicit consumer policy.
caveats: Generating attestations alone provides no benefit without verification, and attestations do not establish that code is secure.
Public repository attestations use public transparency infrastructure; GitHub’s private instance has no transparency log and only federates with GitHub Actions.
The page’s SLSA discussion explicitly refers to v1.0. Its claims should not be silently recast as v1.2 certification.
